title: Why Party Plenums Matter So Much to Xi
gist: Palmer reads the CCP's fifth plenum, unusually centered on 'party self-governance' rather than economic management, as a sign Xi fears his anti-corruption purges are failing, and argues Xi's power rests almost entirely on formal party structures, making retirement risky. The brief also covers Kim Jong Un's Dandong trip signaling interest in China trade, doubts about Chinese backing for Orban at the U.N., an AI-generated film flop, and Chinese video games' global rise.

themes.theme: Fifth plenum agenda shift to party discipline

insights.claim: The CCP's fifth plenum, which traditionally focuses on managing China's semi-planned economy, is instead centered on 'party self-governance,' encompassing anti-corruption and political loyalty to Xi.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Leadership bandwidth is tilted to political control rather than economic policy, lowering odds of major economic initiatives from this plenum.
insights.quote: This week’s agenda is instead centered on “party self-governance,” a formulation that encompasses both anti-corruption efforts and political loyalty to Xi.

insights.claim: Palmer infers the agenda shift suggests Xi may be worried his long-running anti-corruption campaigns and purges are not paying off.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: More purges are likely, extending policy uncertainty for officials and SOE managers.
insights.quote: That shift suggests that Xi might be worried that his long-running anti-corruption campaigns and purges are not paying off.

insights.claim: The generation of leaders Xi elevated to replace the corrupt leadership before him has turned out to be just as corrupt.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Persistent elite corruption undermines governance quality and keeps purge risk high across the system.
insights.quote: Yet the generation of leaders that he has elevated to replace the corrupt leadership that preceded him has turned out to be just as corrupt.

insights.claim: CCP plenums bring together a Central Committee of roughly 200 voting members and about 170 nonvoting alternates, with outcomes typically settled in advance by smaller groups.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Plenum communiques are signals of pre-agreed priorities rather than live debates.

insights.claim: Unlike Mao, who bypassed formal structures, or Deng, who ruled through informal networks with few titles, Xi's power stems almost entirely from his formal position, including control of the CCP's internal security services.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Xi's dependence on office implies he will hold on to formal posts, reducing odds of a managed succession.
insights.quote: As a result, Xi’s power stems almost entirely from his formal position—including, critically, his control of the CCP’s internal security services.

insights.claim: Xi has curtailed rather than cultivated princeling networks and has turned on former allies such as fallen top general Zhang Youxia.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Even senior military figures are not insulated from purges, signaling instability in PLA leadership.

insights.claim: Retirement would be risky for Xi, who is more likely to die in office or be forced out; given his father died at 88 and his mother is near 100, the former could be far off.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Investors should assume long-tenure Xi rule with low near-term succession probability.
insights.quote: Retirement would be risky for Xi, as he is more likely either to die in office or to be forced out of it.
insights.locator: Retirement would be risky for Xi

insights.claim: If Xi is ever forced out, Palmer expects it to come as an unexpected vote at a party meeting rather than a coup, but not at this plenum.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Formal party meetings are the venues where tail-risk leadership changes would surface.
insights.quote: The latter, if it happens, is more likely to come as an unexpected vote at a party meeting than as guns in the night. But it won’t happen at this one.
insights.locator: Retirement would be risky for Xi

insights.claim: Kim Jong Un's trip to Dandong, meeting Wang Huning and touring a bus factory, signaled Pyongyang's eagerness to expand bilateral trade and investment with China.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Watch for expanded China-North Korea cross-border trade and investment.

insights.claim: Chinese companies facing rising domestic labor costs are keen for North Korean infrastructure improvements that could make cross-border factories more efficient.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: North Korea could become a low-cost labor outlet for Chinese manufacturing, a sanctions-related compliance risk.

insights.claim: Kim's efforts to steer the economy toward growth, partly by supporting Russia's war in Ukraine, have been welcome news in Beijing.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Russia-North Korea-China economic links are deepening.

insights.claim: The Trump administration is reportedly encouraging Viktor Orban to run for U.N. secretary-general with supposed Russian and Chinese backing, but Palmer doubts Beijing's support and suspects U.S. officials mistook a noncommittal response for an endorsement.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: China's U.N. institutional strategy favors continuity over disruptors.
insights.quote: My guess is that U.S. officials floated the idea to their Chinese counterparts, received a politely noncommittal response, and mistook it for an endorsement.

insights.claim: China is more likely to follow informal convention and back a Latin American candidate for U.N. secretary-general.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Signals China's preference for protecting its decades of institutional power at the U.N.
insights.quote: China is more likely to follow the informal convention and back a Latin American candidate.

themes.theme: Chinese consumer AI and cultural exports

insights.claim: China's first entirely AI-generated animated feature, Sanxingdui: Future Past, flopped, taking in just $181,000 in its opening weekend.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Consumer appetite for fully AI-generated entertainment is weak, a caution for generative-AI content monetization.

insights.claim: Chinese consumers keen to use AI in everyday life are more reluctant to embrace it in art.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: AI adoption is uneven by use case; creative content faces authenticity resistance.
insights.quote: As keen as the Chinese public is to embrace artificial intelligence for everyday usage, people are more reluctant when it comes to art.

insights.claim: Video games are becoming the exception to China's struggle to turn cultural exports into global hits, with Phantom Blade Zero drawing ecstatic reviews and titles like Black Myth: Wukong and Genshin Impact achieving major success.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Chinese game developers and Tencent are credible global competitors in a growing export category.
insights.quote: But Chinese-made games are now serious global competitors.
